title: From the mailbox to the boutique: Inside L’Occitane’s award-winning direct mail strategy
summary: See how L’Occitane won Best Direct Mail Design at Lob’s Postmark Awards with personalized, lifecycle-driven mail that connects customers to local boutiques.
body_markdown:
L’Occitane customers arrive at their local boutique with an unusual accessory in hand: a piece of the brand’s direct mail.


“Customers actually bring the mailpiece in with them, and there’s this real sense of pride around receiving it,” says Emily McDonald, Senior Manager of CRM at L’Occitane. And it’s not just customers. “Our in-store Beauty Hosts always ask when the next mailpiece is coming.”


This makes it easy to see why L’Occitane took home **Best Direct Mail Design** from Lob’s inaugural Postmark Awards. But the beauty of its direct mail is only part of the story.


Behind each piece is a carefully orchestrated customer experience: lifecycle segmentation, purchase history, local store relationships, personalized creative, and coordination across channels. The goal is to make something that feels unmistakably L’Occitane *and* unmistakably meant for the person receiving it.


## Mail designed around the customer journey


Direct mail has an established place in L’Occitane’s marketing calendar. Every six to eight weeks, the brand sends what it calls its Windows Campaign, timed alongside larger marketing moments and refreshes happening across its website and stores.


McDonald describes these pieces as a kind of “VIP treatment” for core customers. Because mail is a more considered investment, L’Occitane carefully selects the customers most likely to connect with the featured products and content.


That same sense of intention carries into L’Occitane’s triggered mail programs, where personalization gets even more individual. The experience reflects where each customer is in their relationship with the brand, from new and longtime customers to digital shoppers and regulars at a local boutique.


That distinction shapes the design and message a customer ultimately holds in their hands.


## The art of not always selling


L’Occitane’s approach gets even more interesting after the purchase. A transaction isn't treated as the end of the marketing journey. In many cases, the next communication isn't designed to drive another immediate sale at all.


“For some retailers, the mission ends after a transaction is done. For us, we want to carry through that care,” McDonald says. Many pieces don't have a ‘shop now’ or ‘come to the store’ call to action. Instead, it’s ‘we're here for you, thank you for your purchase.’


That philosophy extends to promotions. L’Occitane deliberately avoids becoming overly promotional, particularly when it comes to retention. When the team tested an offer as part of an anti-churn program, it positioned it as a gift rather than simply another discount. The wording mattered enough that the CRM team worked with its retail partners on how the gift should be described so the experience still felt like L’Occitane.


The same thinking appears in event invitations and seasonal communications. The common thread isn't necessarily a sale – it's giving the customer another reason to engage.


## **Dozens of versions, one experience**


The simplicity of the finished mail hides the complexity behind it.


L’Occitane’s program features dozens of possible versions of a piece depending on what someone purchased, where they shopped, their lifecycle stage and other customer data. Product imagery can change. Copy can change. Retail customers can see their nearest boutique. QR codes can lead people into different digital experiences.


Every day, an automated workflow identifies eligible customers based on factors including recency, product purchased and segment, then organizes the data needed to deliver the appropriate version.


The team doesn’t think about direct mail in isolation. Larger brand campaigns set the overarching story, and the CRM team carries that story across channels, adapting the experience based on each customer’s behavior and relationship with the brand.


Jillian Bahr, Associate Manager of CRM, sees cohesion in the finished experience: customers encounter products and copy tailored to them, but the mail still aligns with the larger campaign they may be seeing elsewhere.


So despite all those versions, customers don’t experience complexity. They experience L’Occitane.


## **Making a global brand feel local**


For retail customers, the personalization can extend all the way to their local boutique. A mailpiece might include a map to the nearest location or an invitation to an upcoming store event, creating a direct connection between what arrives in the mailbox and what’s happening in-store.


For Neal Patrick, VP of CRM and Customer Care, that local connection is important: “It's really about the relationship that the customer has, not with us as this faceless organization, but with the Beauty Host that they come in and visit. One of the nice things about direct mail is it gives that opportunity for the physical piece to make the physical connection.”


## **Behind the beauty, plenty of measurement rigor**


The team is equally thoughtful about determining whether all of this is working.


“We hold about 20% as a control group, and then compare the re-buy rate and incremental sales between the control and test groups,” says Tien Xu, Customer Data Analyst. “We also compare by segment, version, channel, and product.” QR codes add another measurement point.


Feedback also comes from the people closest to customers: the Beauty Hosts working in L’Occitane stores. They're the ones who see customers arrive with a mailpiece, hear their reactions and see which invitations actually bring people through the door.


It’s a reminder that even the most sophisticated personalization ultimately comes down to understanding the customer.


## **More moments to make an impression**


L’Occitane isn't finished experimenting with what mail can do. While much of its triggered program currently focuses on post-purchase, the team sees opportunities to expand across the customer journey, from inviting customers to boutique events to following up with useful information and recommendations based on what they’ve purchased.


For a brand being recognized for design, that's perhaps the most interesting part of L’Occitane's story. The beauty of the mail isn't separate from the strategy behind it. It's the final expression of a team thinking carefully about who is on the other end and what would make receiving something from L’Occitane feel a little bit special.
